source.title: A scalable and generic framework for city-wide traffic prediction with large language model
source.authors: Jinlei Zhang; Congwang Deng; Li-Xing Yang; Shu-Xin Zhang; Daoping Wang; Jian-Xi Gao; Zi-You Gao

record.file_problem: The text is a full, unedited Article in Press and warns of possible errors; it contains placeholder publication metadata. Supplementary Tables 6–8 are referenced but not included, so their numerical results are unavailable here.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies LLM depth and model complexity and reports traffic-prediction performance, a different measure and setup from language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study explores model-complexity scaling for traffic prediction. It does not measure held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy, vary training tokens or compute, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The scaling-related results below bear on V6 only; cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (traffic forecasting with a GPT-2 backbone), the study varies backbone depth (1, 2, 4, 6 layers) and swaps in a larger backbone (DeepSeek). It reports downstream MAE, which bears weakly on V6. It fits no power law and reports no pretraining loss, token or compute sweeps. T3 fits better than T2 because the question and measure are task-specific traffic MAE, not an alternative method for the same language-model scaling question. The evidence is qualitative because Supplementary Tables 6–7 are absent.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that more layers or a larger backbone does not guarantee better traffic MAE under their data and compute constraints. They suggest further scaling might help with more data, and call traffic-domain scaling an open, preliminarily explored question.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies LLM depth and backbone in a task-specific traffic-prediction framework and evaluates MAE and computational complexity, rather than measuring language-model held-out cross-entropy across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance depends on LLM depth and backbone; the authors also frame outcomes as conditional on data scale, computational constraints, and training strategy.
record.problems: The relevant numerical results are in supplementary tables not supplied in the text; the scaling summary is qualitative, uses traffic-prediction MAE rather than held-out pretraining loss, and treats layer count as a proxy for model complexity.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-related rows were available in the supplied text. Numerical results referenced in Supplementary Tables 6 and 7 could not be extracted because those tables are absent.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit over parameters, tokens or compute.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
Traffic time-series fine-tuning is a new regime, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
No exponents or fitting choices examined.
No relation of performance to pretraining loss; no smooth or predictable trend assessed over orders of magnitude.

missing.what: Ablation 'Add LLM Layers' (6 GPT-2 layers vs the original 2): performance 'falls short' of the original across datasets.
missing.locator: Results, Ablation study; Fig. 3c; Supplementary Table 3

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is weak and qualitative. The relevant numbers are in Supplementary Tables 3, 6 and 7, which are absent. Data is explicitly a bottleneck, so the results do not bear on V1, whose condition excludes that. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss across parameter count, tokens, and compute, including power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger runs using power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how either quantity grows with compute.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes.
The study measures traffic-prediction performance under changes to LLM depth and backbone; it does not test downstream language-model benchmarks generally or relate performance to pretraining loss.
The study does not fit exponents or compute-optimal splits, vary fitting choices, or test whether fitted power-law curves depart from a single power law.
